posts.post_subject: set up of components - beams crossing??
posts.content_md:
I am trying to set up for split beam transmission and would like to split the object beam to illuminate the object from both left and right (to illuminate object from both sides). If this is done, however, one of the object beams would pass through the reference beam reaching the object. What will this do to? 

My initial problem is my table size - now 18 x 60 in. I have a second 18 x 60 in breadboard that I will add when I add vibration dampening (2 36 x 60 in plywood boards sandwitching tubes or balls). The two breadboard will be attached to top plywood board which will be on tubes or balls which will be on second plywood board all on top of a 6 legged dresser. Currently only 1 breadboard is directly on the dresser. 

Second Question: Can I add the collimating mirror at the distance at which my beam is expanded to the size I want - without regard to the focal length of the lenses. I am able to expand my beam to 9 inches diameter in 30 inches - a point at which the beam is still expanding. Can I place the DLs 31 inches from my Collimating mirror? Is the beam from the CM immediately usable, or must it travel some length (focal length?)

posts.post_subject: set up of components - beams crossing??
posts.content_md:
> **holomark:** I am trying to set up for split beam transmission and would like to split the object beam to illuminate the object from both left and right (to illuminate object from both sides). If this is done, however, one of the object beams would pass through the reference beam reaching the object. What will this do to?

No problem, the beams do not interact as long as there aren't unwanted reflections coming from the optical elements.

> **holomark:** Second Question: Can I add the collimating mirror at the distance at which my beam is expanded to the size I want - without regard to the focal length of the lenses. I am able to expand my beam to 9 inches diameter in 30 inches - a point at which the beam is still expanding. Can I place the DLs 31 inches from my Collimating mirror? Is the beam from the CM immediately usable, or must it travel some length (focal length?)

Theoretically - immediately usable. Practically - dust particles and small defects on the mirror may cause unwanted diffraction. If there is one, you'll need some distance.

posts.content_md: If you place an iris at the diverging optic ahead of the collimating mirror you will eliminate the light on your back wall. That light will show up in the final hologram unless you are very baffled. It takes me longer to set up the baffles than to set up the optics.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.post_subject: set up of components - beams crossing??
posts.content_md:
> **holomark:** If this is done, however, one of the object beams would pass through the reference beam reaching the object. What will this do to?

Nothing. Light does not interact with light and neither beam will detect the presence of the other.

> **holomark:** Can I add the collimating mirror at the distance at which my beam is expanded to the size I want - without regard to the focal length of the lenses. I am able to expand my beam to 9 inches diameter in 30 inches - a point at which the beam is still expanding. Can I place the DLs 31 inches from my Collimating mirror? Is the beam from the CM immediately usable, or must it travel some length (focal length?)

> **holomark:** Why did the relection shrink??? Ok, the mirror was dirty, but that wouldn't seem to cause the problem. It just seems odd that the height of the reflection would change based on the angle of reflection. Would this mean that my CM is not truely collimating?illuminated CM.jpg

First question: Probably, no. Second question: it shrunk because the diverging lens was probably placed too far away.

The collimating mirror is simply a lens "folded out". Consider a point source of light diverging and hitting a lens. Ignore, for this analysis whether or not the light expands around the lens (you can always iris it off). If the light source were placed at infinity, effectively about 10 focal lengths away, then the beam coming out of the lens would focus at the focal length of the lens - f away. As the point source approached the lens, the point where the light focuses on the other side of the lens moves away from the lens. When the point source is 2f away (twice the focal length), then the light focuses at 2f on the other side of the lens. Bring the source even closer and the focused spot moves even further away from the lens. Finally, when the light source is at the focal length at the back end of the lens, the light on the other side is collimated, ie it "focuses" at infinity.

Same with a mirror. Let's say the collimating mirror had a focal length of 25 in (if your mirror is 8 in and it's probably an f#3, it's focal length would be about 25 in). If you place the diverging lens (DL?) over 250 in away from the mirror, the light out of the mirror will focus at 25in. As you bring the DL (I assume that's what a DL is) towards the mirror, the focused spot moves away, but still focuses. Putting a card at some distance from the mirror will give a smaller disk of light than 8in because you're "catching" it in its way to focusing. When the DL is at 50 in from the mirror, the focused spot will also be at 50 in from the mirror (the "2f - 2f" relation). As you bring the DL closer to the mirror, the focused spot moves further out. Finally, when the DL is at 25 in, the beam is collimated.

As for the angle, circular mirrors are designed for on-axis illumination. If your DL was not on-axis (and it really can't be!), then the beam is distorted by an amount depending on the angle between the mirror and the DL. The greater the angle, the greater the distortion. However, the distortion makes the beam thinner (because that's the plane of the mismatch - the plane of the beams), so the height of the beam remains constant and it just gets thinner. If the height also changes, the mirror is not just reflecting side-to-side, it's pointing upwards by some small amount. This might throw off your polarisation. Of course, if your mirror is meant upwards, then the converse is true - the height changes and the width remains. By the way, a note of caution. The greater is this distortion, the greater is the distortion of the image. You should really not have an angle greater than a few degrees between DL and mirror axis.
